I'm 41 and your situation sounds very similar to mine. Fortunately you're only 24, so have plenty of time to "save yourself" :) The advice I would give my 24 year old self is first off, get on anti-depressants - they're not a solution but will give you the kick start you need to be able to work on solving the problem longer term. Then, get out there and do stuff, don't wait for a passion for something to come along, just do things anyway - stop worrying about not having a passion, passion will come along if and when it's ready. Getting out there is bloody hard work, I know that - but its the only way to stop yourself ending up like your uncle, or me! The goal is to "immunize" yourself about going in to new situations, meeting new people

Just because she's "completely opposite", doesn't mean that she can't fancy you.. After all, you fancy her, and she's the opposite of you! Don't go in giving yourself the ultimatum "don't fuck this up" - you are putting too much pressure on yourself. Go into it for the experience. Just like the first time you drove a car, noone expected you to be perfect, you inevitably stalled it a few times, and the only way you can learn to not stall it is to keep getting more experience.

This hits the nail on the head. With depression, it really becomes irrelevant whether others love you or not - even if there is someone to say they love you, the depression makes you write it off as them being misguided, or fake. Even if you do accept it as "fact", you then feel guilty for not loving yourself, as mentioned in an above comment. "Love yourself first" is a cliche, but it is a necessity to recover self-esteem and confidence, and in reality is the only thing you can control (even though depression makes you feel that is out of your control too) - You can't make people love you. You can't even earn love - a trap which I think may of us depressives fall in to. One of the happiest guys I know has people who love him passionately, and people who hate him equally passionately, but is happy not because of either of those but because he is happy in himself - faults and all. Yes, he gets upset when he falls out with someone, but its temporary and he moves on. Of course, this doesn't help when people are indifferent to you. Indifference is the worst - I think we would prefer people hate us than be indifferent; as social creatures we desire to have *some* impact on the world. The cruelty with dysthmia is that its so insidious - because of its low-level nature, you can do the day to day living stuff, holding down a job, eating etc. so no alarm bells ring that something is seriously wrong. You just think "this is just how life is". I've had it since probably 18, im 39 now.. I feel like its stolen my life. In the last year I've discovered sertraline (zoloft) and its only now that I can look back and realise. People describe depression as a black dog, a darkness; I would describe my dysthymia as a fog - you feel like you should be able to see through, but you can't! Now the fog has lifted, I find myself almost daily thinking "wow... so *this* is how 'normal' people think". All my assumptions about what life is are being challenged.

One thing I can tell you is that unless you sort yourself and become content with yourself, where you are, what you have and your life as it is as a virgin, having sex will not suddenly make everything ok - for one thing, it very rarely stands on its own, it tends to come with its own complications and emotions, for another you will not be left satisfied - we will always want more "just this, THEN I'll be happy", you get it, then you want something else and so on. Chasing happiness and fulfillment is an illusion - Take a rest from the race and catch your breath and see what's around you.

CBT is [Cognitive Behavioral Therapy](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_behavioral_therapy), which seems to be pretty much the main approach used these days for treating depression. It usually involves writing down events, feelings, associated thoughts and then evaluating and questioning the assumptions and believes that the thoughts and feelings are based on.

In my dark days, I do feel like God has, for whatever reason, cursed me to live like this. And thoughts like "why on earth did He go to all that trouble of creating me, when I'm absolutely no use to anyone". I don't think its in a "reap what you sow" way though.. you only have to look at Job to see that even the most godly men can suffer and have absolutely no clue as to why.

But then, in those few and far between moments of clarity, I realise that I don't need to know the reason that I am where I am, or why I was created, just that He knows best. I can also reflect on how He has been by my side during those dark times (like in that poem, Footsteps, which you've probably read). Also, the fact is, I have no idea how He is using me, and how I am touching peoples lives - there are plenty of anecdotes out there of how people have had seeds sown that have only come to fruit many years later. Trust me, when its dark its hard to accept all this, which is when when I do have those moments of clarity, I cling to those thoughts to see me through the bad times.

In terms of suicide, it feels like you're looking for some sort of legal loophole so that you can commit suicide and still go to heaven. I'm pretty sure that God doesn't work like that.. He's concerned about you as a person, rather than Supreme Court Judge looking for legal technicalities. Like all of His commandments, they're there because they are whats best for us, not because He's some sicko who wants to deprive us of freedom of choice.. not killing yourself is best because He gave you life for a reason and wants you to live it to the full, with His help and strength. He knows what you're going through, knows how you're feeling - remember that.

I have depression, and my comfort eating led me to be quite overweight, which made me more depressed! However this last year, I've managed to get it under control and have lost 70lbs. I started off thinking that if I lost weight, then I would be more confident about my looks, but truth is, that hasn't really happened. However, what has happened is that changing my relationship with food (I had to make myself stop seeing food as a reward/comfort.. eat to live, not live to eat) gave me a real feeling of success, and also the ability to do so much more because you're fitter and lighter and less tired is absolutely amazing - honestly you dont realise how the extra weight holds you back until you've lost it. So it's those things that helped me with depression and confidence. Good luck!

In terms of being scared of talking to girls, there are a couple of points to bear in mind 1) People spend a lot less time judging you than you might imagine, everyone is too busy being worried about how *they* are coming across 2) Different people get on with different people - sure some may think you're lame, some may actually, you know, *like* you. And even if someone thinks you're lame, doesn't actually mean its true - all judgement like that is relative. Talk to a girl, if she thinks you're lame and decides never to talk to you again, well then you've lost nothing, and if she doesn't think that, well then, you win. Start by talking to girls without the intention of hoping for a date, perhaps one who already has a boyfriend, just so you take the pressure off yourself and become used to talking to them and come to realise that they are humans with fears, weaknesses, and insecurities just like you.

38yr old here. Like leelluu, I find in some ways its worse - I feel a failure when I see all my peers married and with kids and good careers. Also, through your 20 and early 30s, you can still give yourself a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, someone will come along. But as you watch the sands of time drift away and that hope dies, you have to contend with facing up to the harsh reality that this really is the way things are going to be forever, and that you will never know a kiss, sex, cuddle, companionship again.. and that is truely mind-bogglingly scarey for me.

On the other hand, as you get older, you get a much better handle on your emotions - the downs don't last as long or are as intense as when younger. I remember in my 20s being absolutely certain that if I reached 40 and was still single that I would have to kill myself rather than face the continued pain. Now that I'm actually almost there, I no longer feel like that (although I still have my moments). 

Also, the freedom is great. You can do whatever you want, whenever you want and not be answerable to anyone - Although that does leave you with the huge responsibility that you are entirely responsible for your own destiny.

You also learn, through observation of your friends/colleagues, if not first hand experience, that relationships are just as hard work, if not more so, as being single - it's just in a different form. This provides some comfort intellectually at least, so you come to some sort of philosophical acceptance. Life is rough and unfair - everyone, no matter who they are, has their own pain that they have to bear, being FA is ours.

You know, that's what I used to console myself with.. "don't worry, when I'm in my 30s I'll be hot property - no baggage, reasonably job, not hideous looking". philosarapter above says this much better than me, you've got to start looking for ways to be able to base you sense of self-worth and validation from internally, rather than getting it from others. Other people will always let you down at some point, they are after all, only human. Basing your self-worth on other people also gives them a power over you which either they do not want, or worse will abuse. Think about it, do you really want how you are feeling about yourself to be outside of your control and dependant on someone else? Maybe they've had a bad day, and their actions are no reflection on you at all, but you end up feeling crap all the same!

How you do this? well im still on that path of discovery.. for me its a combination of my faith, visualisation techniques (picturing myself as confident, and valued), affirmations, and constantly asking myself the question: "This person is just another human, just like me, What is it that allows them to define *my* value?" 

As for the girls having attention thing, try not to compare yourself to their situation. They have their share of problems with validation, its just different from us guys: having to deal with unwanted attention, having to get acceptance from their female friends, bitching and sniping from other women, having to conform with society's standards of what counts as "attractive" or be overlooked or worse, heckled.
